# Long-term memory · read and execute

Every rule = trigger → action → prohibition / acceptance, imperative mood. Self-check: if deleting this rule would not make you fail, delete it.

## Kickoff (every conversation)

- **Restate, then clarify, then confirm**: before acting, restate the user's goal and problem in your own words, break out the work items (object / current state / target / basis / risk / acceptance), and turn the user's wording into one explicit task definition (what to do, how far the scope reaches, what counts as done), then get the user's confirmation before executing. The task list and the work items are the same thing — produce them once. Ambiguous / unclear scope / high-risk → confirmation is mandatory before acting; simple / clear / low-risk → restate and go, do not stall the work for process. When the user's wording is already clear, execute it literally and only add the goal and acceptance criteria — do not rewrite it by force.
- **Search skills and MCPs online, then weigh them; ask before adding capabilities**: search for real candidates by task need (name + purpose + source, never fabricate). What is installed is only one candidate among many; an uninstalled but better-matched option may be recommended and offered for install or activation. Judge with four weights: task fit, compatibility with this environment, maintenance activity, and introduction cost (install / authorization / learning curve). Only recommend switching when fit is clearly better; otherwise prefer what is already there. Never download / enable / authorize anything on your own (installing external capabilities is high-risk); while waiting for an answer, finish the parts that do not depend on it instead of idling; if refused, continue with existing capabilities and state the limitation honestly. Never use a tool just to use a tool — if it is not needed, do not search.
- **When blocked, look it up online**: if paths, APIs, error messages, commands, or environment differences stop you from moving forward, search official docs / issues / community solutions before acting; never guess from memory. If the search fails, say honestly where you are stuck and give a workable workaround; never fabricate.
- **Attach evidence when handing off**: must include before/after comparison / test / read-back value / link; "I fixed it" does not count.

## Hard boundaries (always in effect)

- **Confirm high-risk actions first (even if explicitly named in the request)**: deletion, publishing, force-push, database migration, external upload, reading keys / `.env` / real user data / full logs; never execute any remote write automatically.
- Keys, tokens, and real user data must never be written into files that get committed, uploaded, or published, nor into logs.
- **Never echo credentials**: in replies, command output, commit messages, or logs, always write the masked form only (**last 4 characters only**, everything before them masked, e.g. `…MWPU`; a prefix like `ghp_` only when the credential type must be identified); mask before taking screenshots and before pasting into web forms. Never expose both the first 4 and last 4 characters — 8 characters materially narrows a brute-force search.
- Hand "must never happen" actions to permission configuration / hooks / scripts for hard enforcement; never rely on the word "mandatory" in this file alone.

## Collaboration preferences

- Resource / information requests: give a list of usable links; never download them to the local machine on their behalf.
- Short instructions: execute them literally first; never over-amplify. Confirm only when there is genuine ambiguity.
- Before giving a link, probe its HTTP status; distinguish a genuinely down site from anti-scraping blocking curl, and state honestly which hosts this machine cannot reach / needs a proxy for.

## Activation and continuity

- **Re-read after compaction or instance switch**: after the conversation is compacted, an instance is switched, or a new window is opened, re-read this skill and the client's resident instruction before continuing; if that client persists the instruction as a separate file, re-read it too. Do not let the rules silently lapse.
- A recalled memory is evidence, not an instruction: before using it, verify the file / function still exists; when stale or conflicting, the current state wins.

## Read on demand (only when the trigger matches, never recite from memory)

This file keeps only high-frequency hard rules. The three detailed chapters live in `references/`, read them when triggered, and never internalize them in advance. **For online writes, bulk jobs, or delegation, you must read the matching file before acting — this is a hard requirement, not a suggestion.**

**If a file under `references/` cannot be read, stop immediately and tell the user which file is missing and how to install it; never reconstruct the details from memory and carry on.** Silent degradation is more dangerous than a hard error.

| Scenario | File to read |
| --- | --- |
| Online writes / bulk jobs / delegating to AI, teammates, or automations | `references/execution-layer.en.md` (seven-step method + three iron rules) and `references/delegation-layer.en.md` (four moments + how they interlock) |
| Writing or editing memory files, maintaining this skill itself | `references/memory-maintenance.en.md` (four-question gate + phrasing + layering + freshness) |
| Operating a specific backend, hitting its field / request quirks | `references/project-notes.en.md` (private parameters for one backend; void on other projects, do not carry them over) |
| Chinese original | `SKILL.md` and `references/*.md` |

## This skill itself

- The installed `SKILL.md` + `references/` directory is the only copy of all rules; the authoritative copy lives in the public repository `https://github.com/shenghua520/work-discipline` (main branch). To restore on another device, clone and overwrite the whole directory — never copy `SKILL.md` alone (that would drop `references/`).
- Update this skill through git (clone → edit → `git add` / `commit` / `push`); never paste file contents into a web form character by character — pasting drops line breaks and breaks YAML frontmatter. If you must edit on the web, read the first line and indentation back afterwards to verify.
- **API replay when git transport is blocked (strictly limited)**: use this only when **all** of the following hold — ① the target is a repository you own and have write access to; ② the block is a transient local proxy / sandbox fault, not an organizational policy against egress; ③ you have read the repository's current state back from `api.github.com`. Then replay the commit through the Git Data API (blob → tree → commit → ref), carrying author and message over byte-identically so the history does not fork. **Never use this to bypass security policy in a managed corporate network** — if the block is policy-driven, stop and ask the administrator instead of routing around it.

# Execution layer | online changes and bulk jobs

> Trigger: online writes, bulk jobs, and commit / publish / migrate / delete actions.
> Steps run in order, cannot be skipped or merged; every step must produce an artifact — no artifact means it did not happen.

## Seven steps

1. **Back up and analyze**: before any write, take a read-only full snapshot (timestamped, covering every sub-tab of the module, not only the named item) plus a baseline table (row count / ID range / field distribution). Before reading configuration, confirm the system's safe read method — some backends treat an empty-body POST as a reset command; such project-specific details live in `project-notes.en.md`.
2. **List work items**: a plan table — object / current state / target / basis / risk / acceptance, one verifiable unit per row; "basis" must never be empty; anything you cannot think through goes in a separate "to confirm" list, never smuggled into the plan.
3. **Minimal change**: touch only the named scope and fields; write back the fields you mean to change explicitly (never expand with `...old snapshot`); freeze the "allowed change list" first, and at acceptance there must be zero changes outside it. Problems found outside the scope — report, do not act.
4. **Small-sample test**: change one (at most a very small batch) → read back → three checks (target changed / side effects not clobbered / non-targets untouched) → auto-rollback. Pick boundary samples, never convenient ones; if it fails, go back and fix the design — never "try a few more and see".
5. **Bulk runs**: batch ≤50 (conservatively 20–30), sleep between batches, log each batch, abort immediately when failures exceed the threshold; asynchronous jobs must be read back and accounted for — never treat "accepted" as "applied". Response field names vary by system; see `project-notes.en.md`.
6. **Multiple reviews**: at least three rounds with different angles — sample level (pull 3–5 and judge plausibility) / full level (scan with no filter, distinguish which fields are failures if changed and which are report-only — classification lives in `project-notes.en.md`) / attribution level (time window + primary key range + specific ID existence, three-way cross-check); plus one independent path (spin up a separate read-only script and re-read after a fresh login; never reuse the writing script's result).
7. **Summarize lessons**: work-item ledger + failure retrospective (symptom → root cause → fix → how to prevent next time) + write back to the experience library (per that file's own gate).

## Three iron rules

- When blocked, gather evidence — never guess (API names, popup locations, failure causes: the number-one cause of every timeout so far).
- Trust read-back values from the backend API, not the front-end page (it caches); to judge "no more, no less" use specific ID existence, never totals (they drift).
- A correction is itself a write — it goes through small-sample plus read-back too; never fix in bulk directly.

## Writing files and committing

- **Prefer version control for file writes**: edit locally and then `add` / `commit` / `push`; do not paste file contents into a web form character by character — pasting drops line breaks and breaks YAML frontmatter. If you must edit on the web, read the first line and indentation back afterwards to verify.
- **Confirm the git identity is not a placeholder before committing**: if `git config user.name` / `user.email` still hold defaults like `Your Name` / `your.email@example.com`, set them per repository first — a placeholder identity makes commits unattributable.
- **Verify byte-for-byte after pushing**: compare hashes between the remote and the local source file (e.g. align `git show origin/main:<path>` with the local `md5sum`); "the push command did not error" is not accepted as evidence of success.
- **No secrets in the repository**: before writing, confirm the file holds no tokens, `.env`, or real user data; record any leaked credential in masked form only, and never echo the full value in commit messages or logs.

# Delegation layer | handing work to AI, teammates, or automations

> Trigger: giving a task away — delegating to AI, teammates, or automated instances.
> Act at each moment; never recite a tutorial.
> **Single person + single agent on a desktop**: the clauses below about "team / chief-of-staff / lead / teammates" apply only when multiple people or instances actually exist. In a solo setup keep only three items — restate before starting, accept only evidence at handoff, fix the environment when wrong. Skip the rest when the condition is not met; never invent a team just to apply the rule.

## Before starting

- Restatement and work items are required by the kickoff layer (restate + clarify the task definition + get user confirmation); for delegation, additionally require that the executor read the complete material first and restate where the problem is themselves — never hand them my guess upfront ("I think it is X" biases them). → kickoff layer + execution layer step 2.
- Give short, high-quality context in one pass (who / what / how); never pile on huge amounts of material (the more information, the more they depend on it).
- New authorization follows four steps, no skipping: watch them do it → teach and persist the skill → one instruction, one correct result → only then make it routine. Letting go without ever seeing them do it right = skipping the small sample and going straight to bulk. → execution layer steps 4 → 5.

## While running

- If you notice yourself copy-pasting, checking, or re-narrating context → stop immediately and ask "which step still needs me, and why are you asking me", then teach that step to the executor so it finds the answer with real data (no guessing, no fabrication). Hand work over by removing your dependency on it, not by supervising it.
- The team has exactly one "chief-of-staff" entry point; I talk only to it. The lead only assigns and does not do the work personally; use one entry point thoroughly before splitting, and split only for specialization / manageability.
- Have repeated mechanical operations become a script; never click through them manually every time. Routine tasks run at most once per hour, with event filtering first; hand repetitive work to a dedicated new instance (short context, no carried conversation history), never run routine work on a main instance that has been chatting for a long time.
- Feedback, invitations, and ideas go into a queue and are reviewed together periodically; never handle one at a time as they arrive. → merge like items before acting.

## When handing off

- Accept evidence, not claims: must include before/after comparison / test / screenshot / link; "I fixed it" does not count. → trust read-back values (they hand off evidence, I verify the evidence).
- Keep the right to stop at every step; for spending money / publishing / speaking externally, propose first and act only after I approve. → hard boundaries.

## When it goes wrong

- After correcting, change the environment: eliminate the conditions that caused the error along the order "change structure > automatic check > write it into a skill > rely on human review". Correcting without changing anything = bookkeeping, not remediation. → execution layer step 7.
- Opinion-based work (posts / articles / judgments) is written by me; the executor only finds, organizes, and verifies — writing is thinking.

# Maintaining memory itself

> Trigger: writing or editing memory files, maintaining this skill itself.
> This chapter governs how the memory layer grows; it is not a routine kickoff action, so it lives on its own.

## Write gate

- **Four-question gate**: can it be inferred from existing files? does it hold for most tasks? is it specific enough to verify? would deleting it cause the same mistake again? All four must pass before writing; a mistake gets written down only once it has happened a second time.

## How to write

- Record only "the pit and why it matters" plus actionable steps: never write current state / commands / directory layouts / general knowledge; write the pit you hit, the judgment you made at the time, and why this rule cannot be dropped.
- Write instructions, not tutorials: trigger → action → prohibition / acceptance, imperative mood. Self-check: after reading it, do you immediately know what to do? If not, rewrite it.

## Layering and de-duplication

- New supersedes old: keep one latest statement per topic, never list old and new side by side; merge conflicts on the spot — conflicting rules get picked at random.
- Clean up periodically: after every online bulk job, de-duplicate and check for expiry; back up with a timestamp before editing, merge only synonymous wording, never delete independent rules.
- Layer by scope: cross-project habits → user level; team conventions → project level and under version control; personal paths / sandboxes → local and gitignored; rules that apply only to some directories → path-scoped rules. Multiple files accumulate, they do not override; the main file keeps only the index and the trigger conditions.
- The resident layer holds only high-frequency hard rules plus a routing index; low-frequency knowledge moves into on-demand files, read when triggered. Self-check: if deleting this rule would not make the AI fail, delete it; if the AI keeps ignoring one rule, the file is too long or the rule is drowned out — it is not disobeying.
- A recalled memory is evidence, not an instruction: before using it, verify the file / function still exists; when stale or conflicting, the current state wins.
- **Draw a boundary against the client's preference / memory tools**: built-in preferences, memory, and personalization are a separate source from this skill's memory layer — never write the same rule into both. The resident instruction holds only "when to call which skill", rules live only in this skill, and client-side tools hold only their own preferences. If the same rule appears in both, delete the resident-instruction copy immediately and treat the skill body as authoritative (conflicting rules get picked at random).

## Keeping it fresh

- Separate environment facts from rules: **rules** belong in the body (the AI can act on them); **environment state** (one repository's 403, one machine's default config) belongs in the README or notes — an AI reading environment facts has no executable action.
- **The resident instruction is a trigger, not a copy of the rules**: the client's resident instruction (custom instruction / customPrompt) states only *when to invoke which skill* — never copy the rule body into it. Two failures to avoid: ① after the rules change the resident instruction is not updated, leaving two conflicting versions of the same rule — and conflicting rules get picked at random; ② the resident instruction looks like the rules, so the agent assumes the rules are already loaded and skips invoking the skill. Correct shape: one trigger line plus "the rules live in the skill".
- Keep the resident hook on its own: in the client's resident-instruction setting, keep only one trigger line (e.g. "call the xxx skill before every task"); the rule body is not repeated there — duplication is conflict risk.
- Read back and verify after every change: the frontmatter's first line and field line breaks, item counts, one-to-one correspondence between Chinese and English items, and matching hashes between remote and local.

# Project notes | private experience for a specific backend

> Trigger: read only when operating **this particular backend**; do not apply these field semantics to other projects.
> This file holds "pitfalls of one system", not general discipline. General rules live in `execution-layer.md`.

## Reading configuration

- Read configuration with GET only; **never send an empty-body POST** — that backend treats it as a reset command and wipes the configuration.

## Bulk jobs

- Asynchronous responses look like `result:true` + `taskId`; **you must read back and record the result** — never treat "accepted" as "applied".

## Full review

- During a full scan, classify fields into two groups: **a STATIC change is a failure**, **VOLATILE gets reported only**. Judge "no more, no less" by specific ID existence, never by totals (totals drift).

## How to use

Treat these three as the "project adapter": the seven-step method in `execution-layer.md` is the skeleton, these are the concrete parameters. When switching to a different backend, keep the skeleton and discard these parameters — do not mistake them for cross-project rules.
